procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order, dated September 14, 1965 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 268 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Appeal No. 268 of 1962 in the Patna High Court against the judgment of the Special Judge. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellant under s. 411 I.P.C. but confirmed his conviction under s. 5 (2) of the Act and reduced the sentence awarded by the Trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the repeal of s. 5(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, which provided for a presumption of guilt, invalidated a conviction that was based on it and pronounced before the repeal.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a Special Judge on March 31, 1962, under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
This conviction was based on a statutory presumption of guilt found in s. 5(3) of the Act.
While the appellant's appeal was pending before the High Court, Parliament repealed s. 5(3) on December 18, 1964.
The High Court, hearing the appeal after the repeal, still invoked the presumption from the repealed s. 5(3) and upheld the conviction.
The appellant argued that since the presumption was a procedural rule and had been repealed, the High Court could no longer apply it.
law: The Court acknowledged the general principle that alterations in procedural law are typically retrospective in character.

However, the Court cited an equally important counter-principle: a statute should not be interpreted to create new disabilities or invalidate transactions that were already complete when the new law came into force.

The synthesis of these principles is that while pending cases are governed by new procedures, any procedure that was correctly adopted and concluded under the old law cannot be reopened or invalidated by the new procedure.
application: The Court applied the second principle to the case. It noted that the appellant's trial and conviction by the Special Judge occurred on March 31, 1962, long before the repeal of s. 5(3) in 1964.
Therefore, the use of the presumption by the trial court was a procedure that was "correctly adopted and concluded under the old law."
The subsequent repeal of this procedural rule could not retrospectively make the original conviction, which was valid when pronounced, illegal or defective.
The High Court, in reviewing the appeal, was correct to consider the law as it existed at the time of the trial to determine the legality of the original conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the repeal of the procedural rule (the presumption of guilt) did not invalidate a conviction that was pronounced before the repeal. The conviction was based on a procedure that was valid and complete under the law at the time of the trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether the charge was defective and invalid due to insufficient particulars, especially when the appellant did not raise this objection during the trial or before the High Court.

facts: The appellant argued that the charge was defective because it did not specify the amounts of the bribes or the names of the persons from whom they were taken.
The appellant did not raise this objection at any point during the trial or in the High Court.
The court found that the record showed the appellant understood the case against him and had adduced all the evidence he wanted to present in his defense.
law: Section 225 of the Criminal Procedure Code states that an error or omission in a charge is not considered material unless the accused was in fact misled by it, and this has resulted in a failure of justice.
application: The Court determined that the absence of sufficient particulars does not automatically invalidate a charge, though it may be a ground for requesting more details.
Since the appellant never complained that he was misled by the lack of particulars and the record indicated he understood the case, the conditions of Section 225 were not met.
The Court concluded that the appellant was not misled and no failure of justice occurred.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that in view of the appellant's failure to object earlier and the provisions of Section 225 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the charge was not defective.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the repeal of s. 5(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, which provided for a presumption of guilt, invalidated a conviction that was based on it and pronounced before the repeal.
appellant_arguments: The presumption of guilt under the repealed s. 5(3) was a rule of procedural law.
Alterations in procedural law are retrospective in character.
Since the law was repealed while the appeal was pending in the High Court, the presumption was no longer available to the prosecution, and the High Court should not have invoked it.
respondent_arguments: While new procedures apply to pending cases, procedures correctly adopted and concluded under the old law cannot be reopened.
The appellant's conviction was pronounced by the Special Judge long before the amending Act repealed s. 5(3).
Therefore, the conviction, which was validly pronounced under the old law, does not become illegal or defective due to a subsequent procedural amendment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the charge was defective and invalid due to insufficient particulars, especially when the appellant did not raise this objection during the trial or before the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The charge was defective as it lacked specific particulars of misconduct, such as the amounts taken as bribes and the persons from whom they were taken.
This lack of particulars deprived the appellant of the opportunity to rebut the presumption of guilt under s. 5(3) and prove his innocence.
respondent_arguments: The appellant never complained in the trial court or the High Court that the charge lacked necessary particulars.
The record shows the appellant understood the case against him and was not misled in his defense.
Under s. 225 of the Criminal Procedure Code, an error or omission in the particulars of a charge is not material unless the accused was actually misled and it caused a failure of justice.
The absence of particulars does not invalidate the charge, though it could have been a ground for asking for better particulars during the trial.

cases.principle: As a general rule, an amended law relating to procedure operates retrospectively.
A statute should not be so construed as to create new disabilities or obligations or impose new duties in respect of transactions which were complete at the time the amending Act came into force.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Although amended procedural laws generally apply retrospectively to pending cases, this principle does not apply to procedures that were correctly adopted and concluded under the old law; such concluded procedures cannot be reopened for the purpose of applying the new procedure.
obiter: As a general rule, an amended law relating to procedure operates retrospectively.
A statute should not be so construed as to create new disabilities or obligations, or impose new duties in respect of transactions which were complete at the time the amending Act came into force.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A conviction that was validly pronounced under the procedural law existing at the time of trial is not rendered illegal or defective by a subsequent amendment to that procedural law. While amended procedural laws generally apply retrospectively to pending cases, this principle does not extend to reopening procedures that were correctly adopted and concluded under the old law. Similarly, a charge that contains the essential elements of the offense is not invalidated by a lack of specific particulars, although such a lack may be a ground for the accused to request better particulars during the trial.
legal_tests_applied: The general rule that amended procedural law operates retrospectively is qualified by the principle, embodied in s. 6 of the General Clauses Act, that a statute should not be construed to create new disabilities or obligations for transactions that were complete when the amending Act came into force.
The principle that whatever procedure was correctly adopted and concluded under an old law cannot be opened again for the purpose of applying a new procedure.
The distinction between a circumstance that invalidates a charge versus one that merely serves as a ground for asking for better particulars.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's conviction was pronounced on March 31, 1962, long before the amending Act repealed s. 5(3) on December 18, 1964. Therefore, the conviction, being a procedure correctly concluded under the old law, could not be invalidated by the subsequent procedural amendment.

The lack of specific particulars in the charge, such as the amounts taken as bribes and the persons from whom they were taken, does not invalidate the charge itself, as it clearly stated that the appellant accepted illegal gratification and obtained pecuniary advantage by corrupt means.
why_respondent_won: The trial and conviction of the appellant were completed when s. 5(3) was still operative, making the conviction a 'transaction which was complete' and thus immune from subsequent changes in procedural law.

The court determined that the alleged defect in the charge was not a fatal flaw that would invalidate the conviction, but rather a matter that could have been remedied by a request for better particulars during the trial.
policy_considerations: A statute should not be construed to impose new duties or create new disabilities in respect of transactions which were complete at the time the amending Act came into force, ensuring legal finality for concluded proceedings.
